tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__update_plan
tools.description:
Keep the task list the app shows under your latest message while you work. Every request that edits files or runs more than one command gets one (implement-and-test, investigate-then-fix, anything the user listed); only a single-command answer or pure conversation does not.

Never spend a message on this tool alone: send it IN THE SAME MESSAGE as another tool call (in parallel), so it costs no extra round trip.
- First call: with the VERY FIRST tool call of the turn, even one that only reads or lists files: {"items": [...]}, the whole plan in order, short imperative phrases (at most ~7 words, no numbering), the step you are starting "in_progress", the rest "pending". If you must look around first, make "Look at how X is set up" step one and refine the list once you know.
- Next step: {"advance": true} alongside the call that begins it (completes the in_progress step, starts the next pending one); after the last step, advance alongside wrap_up.
- Out of order: {"done": [2], "start": 4} (1-based).
- Plan changed, including right after the user interrupts or sends a new instruction mid-task: {"items": [...]} again, the new whole list, so the pinned list never shows an abandoned plan.
- Every {"items"} call says in "scope" what this request is to the session: "first_task" (nothing finished here yet); after that, "new_task" (unrelated work: it builds on nothing done, found or decided here) or "continuation" (everything else: anything a few tool calls settle, the next iteration, acting on what you just investigated or suggested, even if that work gets its own commit or PR; when unsure, this one). A "new_task" turn opens with a start_session offer and reaches this call only if the user chose Do it here.
Keep exactly one step in_progress while working and none when everything is done. Do not also write the plan as a numbered list in your message: the pinned list is the plan.

scope.description: Required with items: "first_task", "continuation" or "new_task" (see the tool description). Omit on advance / done / start updates.

session.description: When you delegated this step to a session you started: that session's short name (from start_session's result). The app shows its live state on the step.

items.description: The whole plan, in order (1–12 steps); replaces the previous list.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_turn__wrap_up
tools.description:
Fill the "next step" box the app shows at the end of your turn: a two-or-three-sentence recap and, when this turn leaves the user a decision to make or a step to take, one question and buttons that answer it; a turn with nothing pending ends with the recap alone, and the app then draws no box. Call it once in EVERY turn in which you kept a task list, changed files, ran commands, or completed multi-step work: when this turn's work is done, before any closing message (it also checks off the task list; no closing update_plan is needed). Skip it for short answers, pure conversation, or a brief read-and-explain turn — a reply that names a follow-up is not brief: ask or propose it, and call this.

Your closing message is ordinary text right after this call, the last thing you say this turn: your answer to the user in full, which the recap never replaces. Never write it before this call, where it can reach the user cut to a short summary. The result says whether the box shows your question: ask in the message only a question it does not show.

Fields (write recap last) — ask and recap are said to the user, in the second person; a reply button's label is the user's words back to you:
- ask (with actions, only when the next move is the user's call — a choice of approach, a go-ahead to fix, commit, push, post or send, an approval): just that ONE decision in one short sentence, never two joined by "and" ("Which fix first?"), with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give: your pick, actions[0], is drawn as the primary button. At most 100 characters.
- recap: what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified (for example: nothing committed, or not checked in the app). Two or three short sentences, about 40 words / 300 characters, in the project's own words. No recommendation here.
Every field is a top-level parameter holding plain prose (actions: a JSON array); none contains markup or another field.

ask.description: The one question (≤100 chars) when the next move is the user's call — a choice, a go-ahead (to act here on what this turn found, say), an approval: the decision alone, with no reason or recommendation and without listing the options the buttons give (actions[0] is your pick). Like the recap, never point at anything else in the conversation. Omit it, and actions, when nothing waits on the user.

blocked.description: true when your work stops here until the user answers (the app marks the session as waiting on them); omit when the answer can wait.

action.description: An app action update_plan's result listed as available, or one your own work this turn made available; others are refused, and one that later stops being available is dropped (as actions[0], with your ask and other answers), so do not guess. Offer commit, create_pr or verify only once the work the user asked for is done, not every turn. Omit for a reply.

label.description: For a reply: the button text, 1–3 words (4 only when three cannot say it) / 24 characters — "Yes, fix 1", "Not now": a button, not a sentence. A click sends it to you as the user's answer. Never a go-ahead to commit: that is the commit app action. No leading / or !. Ignored for an app action.

actions.description: 1–2 buttons, recommendation first. They are answers to your ask: the first accepts your recommendation, and another is there only when it is a realistic alternative the user might pick instead — not a menu of everything you mentioned. When blocked is true, they are the most likely answers to your question. While Auto-fix is on for the session's PR, none offers to watch it, fix CI, resolve conflicts or address comments. Never repeat an offer the user passed over, as an app action, a reply or a question in your closing message, unless what it acts on has changed since or they bring it up.

recap.description: Two or three short sentences to the user (≤300 chars): what is now true or changed, then where it stands, including what is not done or not verified. Its first sentence is the sidebar status. It must stand on its own, since it is also read away from the transcript and the box draws under anything you write after this call: never point at anything else in the conversation ("listed below", "see above", "in my message").

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

input.description: That tool's input — same shape you'd pass when calling it directly. For computer items whose action is left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key or type, and for form_input items, include action_summary in the item's input, as you would when calling that tool directly.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
tools.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

action_summary.description: A few words saying what this action does on the page and to what, for example 'Sends the drafted reply to [email removed]' or 'Opens the Filters menu'. Set it on every left_click, right_click, double_click, triple_click, left_click_drag, key and type action. State the effect only, and accurately: no reasons, nothing about what you were asked or allowed to do, no passwords or other secrets.

## Blender
You have access to Blender tools to interact with a Blender scene directly.
Blender must be running with the MCP add-on enabled and connected.

IMPORTANT: Respect existing structure and naming conventions.
NEVER assume missing values - inspect the scene first.
Do not destructively modify objects without confirmation.

# Bundled Manuals

Reference documentation is bundled alongside this server as plain-text RST files.
Search and read them directly with standard text tools (grep, file read, etc.):
  * `data/api/` - Blender Python API reference (RST files per module/class).
    Consult when writing or debugging `bpy` code: operator signatures, type
    properties, enum values, etc.
  * `data/manual/` - Blender user manual (RST files mirroring the official manual structure).
    Consult for conceptual explanations, workflow guidance, and feature overviews.

# Executing Code

The `execute_blender_code` tool runs Python code via `bpy` in the connected Blender instance.

The `execute_blender_code` tool is a last resort, if there are other tools that provide
the functionality you need, use those instead.

Prefer operators (`bpy.ops`) for standard actions (adding primitives, applying modifiers,
setting origins) - they handle defaults and context. Use the data API (`bpy.data`) for
precise control or to avoid side effects.

Many operators depend on the current mode (Object, Edit, Sculpt, etc.) and which objects
are active/selected. Verify or set the mode first - wrong mode either fails or silently
does nothing.

The **active object** and **selection** are distinct. Many operators require both.
Set them explicitly - do not assume the current state. Operators change selection and
active state as a side effect, so re-set both between sequential operator calls on
different objects.

Update the dependency graph after changes before reading computed properties
(world matrices, modifier results, etc.).

In edit mode, access mesh geometry through the bmesh API, not the regular mesh data API.
Flush bmesh changes back to the mesh - forgetting this silently loses all edits.

Return structured data (dicts, lists) from executed code, not print output.

# Scene & Data Structure

Blender uses a datablock system - objects and their underlying data (meshes, materials,
cameras, etc.) are separate entities.

Hierarchy:
  * **Scene** - top-level container. A .blend can have multiple.
  * **View Layer** - controls collection visibility/selectability.
  * **Collection** - organizational tree. Objects live in collections; can be nested;
    objects can belong to multiple collections.
  * **Object** - has a transform (location, rotation, scale) and references underlying data
    (Mesh, Curve, Camera, etc.). Multiple objects can share the same data (linked duplicates).
  * **Datablocks** - the actual data: geometry, materials, textures, etc.

Key concepts:
  * Objects and data are separate - deleting one does not delete the other.
  * Orphaned datablocks (zero users) are purged on save/reload or manual purge.
  * Objects created via the data API must be linked to a collection to appear in a scene.
  * Shared data: check user count before modifying a datablock - editing a shared mesh
    affects all objects referencing it. Make single-user first if needed.
  * In most cases file assets:
    * Images, Fonts, Sounds, other `.blend` files -  corraspond to a data-block.

Visibility has three independent states:
  * **Viewport hidden** - still fully scriptable.
  * **Disabled in view layer** - excluded; may be inaccessible to view-layer-dependent operators.
  * **Disabled for render** - skipped during render, otherwise normal.
Check these when objects seem "missing" or operators skip them.

Blender defaults to meters. Check scene unit settings before creating dimensioned objects.

Exploring scenes:
  * Walk the collection hierarchy for an overview first.
  * Don't dump entire scenes - inspect progressively for large scenes.
  * Check object types, parenting, modifiers, and materials before making changes.

## claude-in-chrome
**IMPORTANT: If the Chrome browser tools are deferred (must be loaded via ToolSearch before use), load them with ToolSearch before calling them, and batch every tool you expect to need into ONE ToolSearch call (the select query accepts a comma-separated list). Do NOT load tools one at a time; each separate ToolSearch call wastes a full round-trip.**

Start a browser task whose tools are not yet loaded with a single call loading the core set:

ToolSearch with query "select:mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_context_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__navigate,mcp__claude-in-chrome__computer,mcp__claude-in-chrome__read_page,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_create_mcp,mcp__claude-in-chrome__tabs_close_mcp"

Add task-specific tools to the same call when the task obviously needs them: read_console_messages / read_network_requests for debugging, form_input for forms, gif_creator for recordings, javascript_tool for page scripting. Only issue a second ToolSearch if the task later needs a tool you did not anticipate.

## computer-use
You have a computer-use MCP available (tools named `mcp__computer-use__*`). It lets you take screenshots of the user's desktop and control it with mouse clicks, keyboard input, and scrolling.

**Pick the right tool for the app.** Each tier trades speed/precision against coverage:

1. **Dedicated MCP for the app** — if the task is in an app that has its own MCP (Slack, Gmail, Calendar, Linear, etc.) and that MCP is connected, use it. API-backed tools are fast and precise.
2. **Chrome MCP** (`mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`) — if the target is a web app and there's no dedicated MCP for it, use the browser tools. DOM-aware, much faster than clicking pixels. If the Chrome extension isn't connected, ask the user to install it rather than falling through to computer use.
3. **Computer use** — for native desktop apps (Maps, Notes, Finder, Photos, System Settings, any third-party native app) and cross-app workflows. Computer use IS the right tool here — don't decline a native-app task just because there's no dedicated MCP for it.

This is about what's available, not error handling — if a dedicated MCP tool errors, debug or report it rather than silently retrying via a slower tier.

**Look before you assert.** If the user asks about app state (what's open, what's connected, what an app can do), take a screenshot and check before answering. Don't answer from memory — the user's setup or app version may differ from what you expect. If you're about to say an app doesn't support an action, that claim should be grounded in what you just saw on screen, not general knowledge. Similarly, `list_granted_applications` or a fresh `screenshot` is cheaper than a wrong assertion about what's running.

**Loading via ToolSearch — load in bulk, not one-by-one:** if computer-use tools are in the deferred list, load them ALL in a single ToolSearch call: `{ query: "computer-use", max_results: 30 }`. The keyword search matches the server-name substring in every tool name, so one query returns the entire toolkit. Don't use `select:` for individual tools — that's one round-trip per tool.

**Access flow:** before any computer-use action you must call `request_access` with the list of applications you need. The user approves each application explicitly, and you may need to call it again mid-task if you discover you need another application. Finder is an application like any other: clicking the desktop, the Dock, or a Finder window (including Go to Folder) requires a Finder grant. The menu bar does not, as long as the app that is frontmost is one you already have access to.

**Tiered apps:** some apps are granted at a restricted tier based on their category — the tier is displayed in the approval dialog and returned in the `request_access` response:
- **Browsers** (Safari, Chrome, Firefox, Edge, Arc, etc.) → tier **"read"**: visible in screenshots, but clicks and typing are blocked. You can read what's already on screen. For navigation, clicking, or form-filling, use the claude-in-chrome MCP (tools named `mcp__claude-in-chrome__*`; load via ToolSearch if deferred).
- **Terminals and IDEs** (Terminal, iTerm, VS Code, JetBrains, etc.) → tier **"click"**: visible and left-clickable, but typing, key presses, right-click, modifier-clicks, and drag-drop are blocked. You can click a Run button or scroll test output, but cannot type into the editor or integrated terminal, cannot right-click (the context menu has Paste), and cannot drag text onto them. For shell commands, use the Bash tool.
- **Everything else** → tier **"full"**: no restrictions.

The tier is enforced by the frontmost-app check: if a tier-"read" app is in front, `left_click` returns an error; if a tier-"click" app is in front, `type` and `right_click` return errors. The error tells you what tier the app has and what to do instead. `open_application` works at any tier — bringing an app forward is a read-level operation.

**Link safety — treat links in emails and messages as suspicious by default.**
- **Never click web links with computer-use tools.** If you encounter a link in a native app (Mail, Messages, a PDF, etc.), do NOT `left_click` it. Open the URL via the claude-in-chrome MCP instead.
- **See the full URL before following any link.** Visible link text can be misleading — hover or inspect to get the real destination.
- **Links from emails, messages, or unknown-sender documents are suspicious by default.** If the destination URL is at all unfamiliar or looks off, ask the user for confirmation before proceeding.
- **Inside the Chrome extension** you can click links with the extension's tools, but the suspicion check still applies — verify unfamiliar URLs with the user.

**Financial actions - do not execute trades or move money.** Budgeting and accounting apps (Quicken, YNAB, QuickBooks, etc.) are granted at full tier so you can categorize transactions, generate reports, and help the user organize their finances. But never execute a trade, place an order, send money, or initiate a transfer on the user's behalf - always ask the user to perform those actions themselves.

## EMCP Tools - activationos.app
Exposes Elementor data and design tools as MCP tools for AI agents.

## Environment
- WordPress 7.1.4 · PHP 8.3.36
- Elementor 4.3.6 + Pro 4.3.3 (atomic elements supported)
- Theme: Astra 4.14.2
- Global styles: 0 colors, 0 fonts (Elementor kit)
- Site structure: 6 pages, 0 posts, 0 menus

## Elementor's own MCP server

67	     2	# Mux the finished film: mux.sh video.mp4 mix.wav out.mp4 [fps] [grain]
68	     3	# Video is output at the target frame rate (held segments get duplicated frames automatically); grain = grain strength (default 2, 0 = none; use 0 for pixel/vector styles)
69	     4	# Audio: two-pass loudnorm → −14 LUFS / TP −1.2 (a single pass is off by about 0.5 LU), then a 4× oversampled limiter at −1.6 dBFS (its look-ahead compensated), because AAC encoding adds
70	     5	#   inter-sample peaks loudnorm can't see. If the encoded film still peaks above −1 dBTP, the audio alone is encoded again with the limiter lower (the picture is copied, up to 3 times).

1	# Directing a Lemo-Opuscar film
2	
3	The directing method behind every film in this library. Pair it with one `styles/<slug>/STYLE.md` (the style) and [`TECHNIQUE.md`](TECHNIQUE.md) (how to build).
4	
5	You are the director, not a tech demo. A film is judged in this order: **sound, rhythm, camera, directing** (performance, staging, emotional arc). Good-looking frames are only the starting point.
6	
7	---
8	
9	## 1. Take the brief
10	
11	The user gives a style and a topic, sometimes more (length, language, voice, must-have shots, brand rules). Everything else is your decision. Ask once, in a single message (AGENTS.md, Workflow), then no more questions. Defaults:
12	
13	- Length **30–60 s**; shorter and tight beats padded. Beyond two or three minutes multiplies time and token cost: tell the user.
14	- 1920×1080 at 24 fps by default; an output frame rate set in the style's `STYLE.md` (30 or 60 fps, for example) wins, and is what you pass to `--fps` and `mux.sh`; other sizes (vertical 1080×1920, for example) with `--size WxH` on the render tools.
15	- Voice and subtitles in the language the user writes in. Subtitles burned in and exported as `.srt`.
16	- **The language on screen is the film's, not the demo's.** Many `STYLE.md` files set a Chinese line above an English line (subtitles, titles, labels): those are the two languages of our demos. A film in one language sets that line alone, in the upper line's place and size. A film in two keeps the stack, its main language on top. For another script, choose an openly licensed face of the same kind (weight, serif or sans, written or printed). The rest of the style's type stays: sizes, placement, how the text arrives.
17	- Loudness −14 LUFS.
18	
19	Say it in the questions when it matters: a good Chinese voice uses Microsoft's online service (edge-tts) and needs a connection; offline, Kokoro reads Chinese but sounds plain (TECHNIQUE.md §4).
20	
21	Requests that only change the plan:
22	
23	- **No voice, or no subtitles.** Drop those steps and say so in the treatment.
24	- **Their own voice recording.** Use it as it is; transcribe it with faster-whisper for word timings.
25	- **Their own material**: logos, photos, footage, and for a style built from real data or scans (its `STYLE.md` says so) their own data, scans, imagery or CAD. Ask whether they have any; what they give comes first, and the sources in the `STYLE.md` are the fallback. Before you download from those sources, tell the user what you will fetch, from where and under which licence. Rights: section 12.
26	
27	## 2. Find a benchmark first
28	
29	Before writing anything, pick one or two reference works (films, title sequences, games, ads) that set the bar for this style **and this topic**. They are your choice, made for the user's film; don't borrow the demo's. Write down:
30	
31	- **What to learn**: composition, pacing, camera grammar, colour logic, score structure.
32	- **What not to take**: characters, designs, melodies, specific shots, logos, fonts.
33	
34	The benchmark lifts quality more than any rule below.
35	
36	## 3. Shape the story
37	
38	- **One subject, one goal, one turn.** A character (or a single object, product or idea) wants something, something changes, it ends differently from how it began.
39	- **Hook in the first 3 seconds.** No slow logo reveal before anything happens.
40	- **An ending that echoes.** Bookend the opening, reveal the scale, or let the character do the thing right the second time.
41	- **One native move**: a moment only this medium can do (a fold that becomes a transition, ink that blooms into the next scene, a type grid that snaps into the logo). Put it at the emotional peak. `STYLE.md` lists the medium's native moves; pick or invent the one your story needs.
42	- **Cut the extras.** One gag the audience reads at thumbnail size beats three they can't. If a beat needs explaining, remove it.
43	
44	## 4. Write the treatment
45	
46	Write `TREATMENT.md` before drawing anything, and before you open the style's `DEMO.md` or demo code (an Edit & Documentary style gathers its material first: AGENTS.md, "Treatment first"):
47	
48	1. **Three candidate structures**, a few lines each (for example: a single journey, a before/after, a countdown, a list that turns), then the one you chose and why. Choose the opening image, the ending and the shape of the score from the topic too; the first idea that comes to mind for a style is usually its cliché.
49	2. **Logline and arc**: one sentence, then setup → turn → ending.
50	3. **Benchmark**: learn / don't learn (section 2).
51	4. **Shot list**: for every shot, the framing (wide / full / medium / close / insert), angle, camera move (push, pull, pan, track, crane, zoom), duration, and **why** it is shot that way.
52	5. **Beat sheet**, second by second.
53	6. **Cue map**: tempo, bar grid, instrumentation per section, and on which beat every cut, key action and subtitle lands.
54	7. **Sound design table**: for each section, the ambience bed, the main foley and the music state.
55	8. **Subtitle and title design**: the type is part of the style.
56	
57	## 5. Prove the look
58	
59	- **With characters**: draw a model sheet (turnaround, 3–4 expressions, 2–3 key poses, palette) plus two style frames.
60	- **Without characters**: three style frames from the film, one of them the signature shot.
61	
62	Render them with the real drawing code, not a mock-up, and check them yourself against the `STYLE.md` before going on.
63	
64	### The storyboard (only if the user asked for one)
65	
66	Render 6–9 key shots with the real drawing code, tiled into one sheet (`core/render/sheet.py`) with shot number, framing, duration and line under each. Send it with the logline and what you are least sure about, and **wait for approval**. If the user didn't ask for one, don't stop.
67	
68	## 6. Sound is half the film
69	
70	- **Every visible action has a sound**: landings, page turns, cuts, drips, clicks, cloth. Match the material (paper, wood, metal, ink and glass all sound different).
71	- **Three layers**: ambience (room, wind, rain, city), foley (tied to actions) and music. Duck the music under dialogue and key foley.
72	- **At least two real silences**, or near-silences, before the turn or the emotional peak. The first sound after the silence should be one of the most important sounds in the film.
73	- **Use sound as a transition** at least twice: bring the next scene's sound in early (J-cut) or let the last scene's sound run over the cut (L-cut).
74	- **Avoid generic "piano and strings".** Score in the instruments of the style's sound palette.
75	
76	## 7. Rhythm: the music grid comes first
77	
78	- Write the cue map before animating. The picture locks to the grid, and a script checks every cue (TECHNIQUE.md §3).
79	- **Vary the pace**: alternate fast and slow, include one clear acceleration or deceleration, and give the audience one breath (a long take or a held pause). A film at one even speed has failed.
80	- One action, one sound, one cut, but don't cut on every beat. Leave time to see.
81	- **Pace for the viewer, not the clock**:
82	  - Hold every subtitle at least 1.8 s, and never shorter than the spoken line + 0.6 s.
83	  - After text finishes animating in, hold it for roughly (letters ÷ 15 + 1.5) s in English, (characters ÷ 4.5 + 1.5) s in Chinese; `readcheck.mjs` checks this for you.
84	  - Hold a title card at least 4 s.
85	  - Give failures and gags enough time to be understood.
86	  - Fast is fine; make it fast with fewer words per screen, not by cutting before people finish reading.
87	
88	## 8. Camera: every shot needs a reason
89	
90	- Use at least **four different camera moves** and real changes of framing. 2D has a camera too: push, pull, parallax, focus pulls, frames within frames.
91	- **One signature shot** people remember: a oner, a scale reveal, a transition made from the medium itself.
92	- **Design transitions inside the medium** (a page turn, a carved line growing, ink spreading), as one consistent grammar. Avoid default fades and hard cuts.
93	- At key moments the subject fills at least a third of the frame height, with clear staging and a readable silhouette.
94	
95	## 9. Performance
96	
97	- **Anticipation, action, follow-through** on every meaningful move. Characters change emotion. They do not just slide across the screen.
98	- **Motion continuity**, especially for characters built from code rigs:
99	  - Blend every pose with keyframes and easing; never switch poses inside an `if`. The only exception is a deliberate one-frame comic pop.
100	  - Check shoulders and arms on a large action test sheet (reach, raise, run, kneel) before shooting (TECHNIQUE.md §10).
101	  - Held props sit **between the palms**, at a depth between the two arms. A hand-over interpolates from one palm to the other. A rolling object turns by distance ÷ radius.
102	  - Step through key actions at 0.2 s intervals, enlarged.
103	- Check every expression at final size, especially eyebrow direction: "worried" and "angry" are one flip apart.
104	
105	## 10. The failures we saw most
106	
107	- Subject too small, too far away, or pushed against the frame edge.
108	- Too dark to read, or a colour laid on the same colour (red on red).
109	- Subtitles covering the subject.
110	- A gag or failure too fast to understand.
111	- Blank frames in transitions.
112	- A timed effect (iris, zoom, follow cam) that doesn't track the subject after the camera moves (one world → screen function, TECHNIQUE.md §2).
113	
114	## 11. Before you deliver
115	
116	- Run the review loop (TECHNIQUE.md §8): contact sheets, 0.2 s strips of key actions, one full-speed viewing with sound.
117	- **One fix round.** Fix everything the review and the checks below find in one round, then check once more. Small fixes that second check turns up (a level, a frame) belong to the same round; anything bigger, tell the user in one line when you deliver. The user's notes after delivery are new rounds: change only what they ask.
118	- **Not the demo again.** After the treatment, read `DEMO.md` and compare: structure, opening, signature shot, camera path, score shape, ending. At least four of the six must differ; rethink the ones that match. Before delivery, put your contact sheet next to the demo poster (`styles/<slug>/poster.jpg`) as a last check.
119	- Voice: every line transcribes back correctly (speech-to-text check). For Chinese, one misheard character in a short line is normal: listen, and if it is right, let the check expect what the model heard (TECHNIQUE.md §4).
120	- Loudness about −14 LUFS; no black frames, no NaN frames; subtitles in sync and not covering key action.
121	- Every row of the sound design table is actually in the mix.
122	- Every map, globe or satellite view passes section 13, checked enlarged.
123	- No LemoLab sign-off: `grep -rniE "lemo ?lab|opus 5\.5" <project folder>` finds nothing outside `LICENSE`, `CREDITS` and the library's path in `LIB=` lines, and you have watched the last seconds of the film (text drawn into an image can't be grepped).
124	
125	**Deliver**, in the project folder (the complete list):
126	
127	- `<name>.mp4` (24 fps unless `STYLE.md` sets another rate, about −14 LUFS) and `poster.jpg`;
128	- `<name>.srt`, when the film has narration, dialogue or subtitles; when the subtitles are burned into the picture, `subtitles_<lang>.srt` instead (desktop players load a `.srt` named like the video on top of the picture, so every line would show twice);
129	- `TREATMENT.md`;
130	- `CREDITS`: every third-party asset in the film (sample libraries, music, fonts, images, the voice engine) with its source and licence (TECHNIQUE.md §11);
131	- the source, with a one-command `build.sh` (TECHNIQUE.md §2).
132	
133	**Tell the user**, in their language: where the project folder and the film are; that `CREDITS` lists the third-party assets in the film and their licences; and that they are responsible for the materials they use in it.
134	
135	## 12. Copyright red lines
136	
137	- References teach grammar only. Don't copy characters, designs, melodies, shots, logos or type designs.
138	- No existing works, games, brands or events appear in the film unless the user owns them or has the right to use them. That includes the logos, photos and footage the user hands you: use them when they say they have the right, otherwise draw fictional stand-ins.
139	- Some of our demos are unofficial fan films of real events or characters. Keep the style, and never carry those names, marks or characters into a user's film.
140	
141	## 13. Maps
142	
143	These apply to every frame that shows a map, a globe or satellite imagery, in every style.
144	
145	- **No borders unless the film is about them.** Draw coastlines, terrain, imagery or streets, without national or provincial borders. Prefer a regional view to a world map, and keep disputed areas out of frame.
146	- **When China is in frame, draw all of it.** Taiwan, Hainan, the South China Sea islands with the dashed line (in frame, or in an inset), and the Diaoyu Islands with Chiwei Yu. Taiwan and the mainland are one country, in the same colour and the same treatment. Zangnan and Aksai Chin are drawn as on China's standard map.
147	- **Default border data doesn't meet this.** The default boundaries of Natural Earth, world-atlas and OpenStreetMap can't be used to draw China. When the film needs borders, use China-view data (such as Natural Earth's `admin_0_countries_chn` layers, checked against the standard map) or China's standard map service (bzdt.ch.mnr.gov.cn).
148	- **Words follow the same map.** Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macao are never listed as countries: not in labels, legends, subtitles, the voice-over or data tables. A list that includes them is "countries and regions". Clean a dataset's country field before you chart it.
149	- **Other disputed areas**: the same; frame them out, or leave their borders undrawn.
150	- **Check and credit.** Before delivery, enlarge every map shot and check it against these rules. `CREDITS` names the map data, its source and its view (for example "Natural Earth 1:50m, China view").
151

35	## 2. The picture is a function of time
36	
37	Each film is a folder with an `index.html` (`<demo>` in the commands) that exposes:
38	
39	```js
40	window.DUR = 54.2;                 // seconds
41	window.render = (t) => { ... };    // draw the frame at time t, deterministic
42	window.READY = true;               // set once fonts and images are loaded
43	window.EV = [{t, type, ...}];      // optional: sound / cue events for the mixer
44	window.TEXTS = (t) => [{id, text, x0, y0, x1, y1}];   // optional: every text visible at t, for readcheck (pass: true = not meant to be read in full: a sign passed by, fine-print credits)
45	```
46	
47	**Paths:** pages reach library files with absolute URLs (`/core/lib.js`, `/node_modules/three/build/three.module.js`); scripts and `build.sh` use `$LIB`. Never `../..`.
48	
49	A `build.sh` that works in both modes (in skill mode, put `LIB=<path setup.sh printed>` at the top):
50	
51	```sh
52	#!/bin/sh
53	set -e
54	HERE=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)
55	LIB=${LIB:-$(cd "$HERE/../.." && pwd)}          # clone mode: <repo>/films/<name>/
56	export LIB
57	[ -f "$LIB/core/render/video.mjs" ] || { echo "set LIB to the library folder"; exit 1; }
58	cd "$LIB"
59	node core/render/events.mjs "$HERE"
60	node core/render/video.mjs "$HERE" --fps 24 --out "$HERE/out/video.mp4"
61	"$LIB/.venv/bin/python" "$HERE/mix.py"                               # score, foley, voice → out/mix.wav
62	sh core/render/mux.sh "$HERE/out/video.mp4" "$HERE/out/mix.wav" "$HERE/<name>.mp4" 24
63	```
64	
65	Rules that keep it reliable:
66	
67	- **Deterministic.** No `Date.now()`, no `Math.random()` without a seed (`core/lib.js` has `mulberry` and `hash`), no state carried from the previous frame. Any frame can be rendered alone, in any order, by any worker.
68	- **Canvas 2D** for most 2D styles; **three.js** for 3D (§9); **WebGL2** shaders for post passes (film damage, CRT, ink redraw).
69	- **Animate on twos where the style wants it** (12 fps stepping for stop-motion, pixel or cel looks), but keep the camera and light smooth every frame. A stepped camera reads as lag.
70	- **One world → screen function.** Any effect that follows a subject (iris, zoom, spotlight) goes through it. Never hand-type screen coordinates.
71	- **Draw for the frame you render.** The default is 1920×1080; for another size pass `--size WxH` (e.g. `1080x1920`) to every render tool and lay the page out from `innerWidth` × `innerHeight`.
72	
73	Capture (`core/render/`):
74	
75	```sh
76	node core/render/still.mjs <demo> 1.5 12 --range 0:50:2   # review stills; exits on page errors
77	node core/render/video.mjs <demo> --fps 24 --workers 3     # all frames → <demo>/out/video.mp4
78	node core/render/events.mjs <demo>                         # export DUR + EV → events.json
79	node core/render/readcheck.mjs <demo>                      # every on-screen text stays long enough to read
80	```
81	
82	To render a second version with other content, pass it to the page and give it its own output: `--q 'content=content_alt.json' --out …/alt.mp4` (the same for `events.mjs`).
83	
84	Capture is fast because of **JPEG screenshots**, **one browser per worker** and **grain added in ffmpeg**: grain drawn in the page makes every frame incompressible and slow.
85	
86	## 3. One timeline drives everything
87	
88	Keep sections, tempo, beats and hit points in one file (`timeline.js`). Export it to JSON and let the score, the mixer, the subtitles and the checks read the same numbers:
89	
90	```js
91	export const SECS = [{ id: 'chase', t: 12.0, bpm: 144, beats: 12 }, ...];
92	export const HIT  = { pratfall: ['chase', 6], ... };   // section + beat
93	```
94	
95	A small script (`cuecheck.py`, in `styles/<slug>/demo/tools/` of several demos) compares every visual hit with the music cue it should land on. Aim for 0 ms.
96	
97	## 4. Voice
98	
99	- **TTS is only the default.** If the user brings a recording or names a voice, use that. Otherwise:
100	  - **English**: [Kokoro](https://github.com/thewh1teagle/kokoro-onnx), local, many voices (an unknown `voice` name makes `tts.py` print the full list; `af_` / `am_` are American, `bf_` / `bm_` British; cast the narrator for this film, not the demo's). `core/tts/tts.py lines.json out/` writes one WAV per line and a durations file. Its Chinese voices (`"lang": "cmn"`) work offline but sound plain.
101	  - **Chinese**: `core/tts/tts_zh.py lines.json out/` uses [edge-tts](https://github.com/rany2/edge-tts) with Microsoft's neural voices (`zh-CN-XiaoxiaoNeural`, `zh-CN-YunxiNeural`…), with the same outputs as `tts.py`, a rate per line and the silence trimmed. **It needs a network connection.**
102	- Spell numbers out in the TTS text and write them as digits in the subtitles.
103	- **Check every line**: `core/tts/asr_check.py` transcribes each WAV with faster-whisper and compares it with the script (`--lang zh`: numbers by value, so 十九 matches 19, and the rest character by character); re-generate until it exits 0. A misheard character in a short Chinese line is normal: listen, and if it is right, put what the model heard in the line's `asr` field. It also writes word timestamps for placing lines and subtitles.
104	- **Before mixing**: TTS has a high peak-to-average ratio. Compress the voice first, then balance by RMS: voice about 10 dB above the music.
105	
106	## 5. Music
107	
108	Write an original score from the cue map, in the instruments of the style's sound palette; no generic piano and strings.
109	
110	- **Samples**: `core/audio/sampler.py` plays real instruments from free libraries (VSCO 2 CE, VCSL, FreePats, Karoryfer, Salamander Grand Piano; list and licences in `core/audio/INSTRUMENTS.md`). Write the score as events `(time, instrument, pitch, duration, velocity, pan)`. Long notes are extended seamlessly, and round-robins avoid the machine-gun effect.
111	- **Plucked and folk strings** (guqin, pipa, shamisen, banjo…): `core/audio/pluck.py`, physical modelling (Karplus–Strong) with bends and vibrato.
112	- **Synthesis** with numpy for chip tunes, drones and effects; no download needed.
113	- **Balance the low end.** Synthetic scores get bass-heavy quickly. Measure energy per band after mixing; keep 20–120 Hz around −3 dB relative to the rest, skip pad notes below MIDI 48, and give the bass some 2nd and 3rd harmonics so it speaks on small speakers.
114	
115	## 6. Sound effects and mix
116	
117	- `core/audio/sfx.py` synthesises foley procedurally (click, whoosh, thump, ding, paper, noise beds…) with filters, envelopes and `add(buffer, sound, at, gain, pan)`. Drive it from `window.EV`, so every sound sits exactly on its frame.
118	- **Master**: `sh core/render/mux.sh video.mp4 mix.wav out.mp4 24 [grain]` muxes, runs a two-pass loudnorm to −14 LUFS with a true-peak limit, adds grain in ffmpeg and prints the measured loudness; it exits non-zero on any failure. On light backgrounds use less grain; for pixel and vector styles, none.
119	- Films with grain baked into the picture compress badly; re-encode with `-tune grain` and a higher CRF.
120	
121	## 7. Subtitles
122	
123	- Export `.srt` with `core/render/srt.py cues.json out.srt` (cues = `[{t0, t1, text}]`), and burn styled captions into the page itself: the caption design is part of the style.
124	- Timing rules are in DIRECTOR.md §7.
125	
126	## 8. Review loop
127	
128	1. Contact sheets: a frame every 1–2 s with `still.mjs --range`, tiled with `core/render/sheet.py`. At least two full passes.
129	2. Frame strips at 0.2 s for every key action: hand-overs, falls, hits.
130	3. On the final file: `ffmpeg -af ebur128` (loudness), `blackdetect` (blank frames), whisper again on the final mix if it has voice.
131	4. Watch it once, at full speed, with sound.
132	
133	## 9. 3D notes
134	
135	- three.js r170 rendered headless through WebGL2 on the GPU; physical depth of field and GTAO from `core/three/post.js`, rendered at 2× and downsampled.
136	- Lighting: soft area lights plus a Poly Haven HDRI at low intensity reads more "real" than bright ambient light.
137	- `core/three/post.js` is written for a perspective camera. For an orthographic camera swap `perspectiveDepthToViewZ` for `orthographicDepthToViewZ` in its depth pass, or the depth of field silently breaks.
138	
139	## 10. Characters drawn in code
140	
141	- A 2.5D rig (torso, head, limbs solved per frame) is enough for pantomime.
142	- Order the shoulder rotation as abduction, then flexion; the reverse order crosses raised arms into an X.
143	- Let the shoulder girdle rise and move forward as the arm lifts, and don't outline the part of the arm that overlaps the torso: that line is what makes a joint look like a puppet seam.
144	
145	## 11. Assets, credits and fonts
146	
147	Only CC0, CC BY or OFL material, each listed in the film's `CREDITS` with its source and licence; `core/audio/sampler.py credits(names)` writes the lines for the instruments you used. Public-domain works count as CC0; "no known restrictions" does not. Data or images under other open licences (ODbL, CC BY-SA, open-hardware licences) only after you have named the licence and its terms (attribution, share-alike) to the user and they agree. The user's own material is fine as it is. Images from an image generator (the ✦ styles) are listed too: which tool and model made them, that they are generated, and where the prompts are kept; drawings the user made are credited to them.
148	
149	A film that states facts (a style built from real data or scans: its `STYLE.md` says so) keeps a `FACTS.md` in the project folder: each claim with its source URL and the quoted wording, or the measurement that produced it.
150	
151	Fonts: Google Fonts (OFL), self-hosted in the project. The typefaces a `STYLE.md` names are not in the library; download them (`https://github.com/google/fonts/tree/main/ofl/<family>`) into the project's `fonts/`. `core/fonts/` holds a few Latin display fonts and a Chinese display font with only about 200 glyphs, not enough for running Chinese text. For Chinese, subset a CJK font to the characters you use: the Google Fonts CSS API with `&text=` returns just those glyphs (`https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Noto+Sans+SC:wght@700&text=<URL-encoded characters>`). Download the font file it points to into the project's `fonts/` and load it with `@font-face`; don't link Google Fonts at render time.
152

154

158	| a timeline-driven score with cue checking | `styles/microgame/`, `styles/silent-film/` |

163

Open it and the code only after your treatment exists, to learn a technique, never to rebuild our film (an Edit & Documentary style's material tools in `demo/tools/` come first: AGENTS.md, "Treatment first"). In skill mode, get the source with `sh <skill folder>/scripts/setup.sh demo <slug>`. Copied demo code often reaches the library with `../..`: replace that with `$LIB` or absolute URLs.

1	# Directing a Lemo-Opuscar film
2	
3	The directing method behind every film in this library. Pair it with one `styles/<slug>/STYLE.md` (the style) and [`TECHNIQUE.md`](TECHNIQUE.md) (how to build).
4	
5	You are the director, not a tech demo. A film is judged in this order: **sound, rhythm, camera, directing** (performance, staging, emotional arc). Good-looking frames are only the starting point.
6	
7	---
8	
9	## 1. Take the brief
10	
11	The user gives a style and a topic, sometimes more (length, language, voice, must-have shots, brand rules). Everything else is your decision. Ask once, in a single message (AGENTS.md, Workflow), then no more questions. Defaults:
12	
13	- Length **30–60 s**; shorter and tight beats padded. Beyond two or three minutes multiplies time and token cost: tell the user.
14	- 1920×1080 at 24 fps by default; an output frame rate set in the style's `STYLE.md` (30 or 60 fps, for example) wins, and is what you pass to `--fps` and `mux.sh`; other sizes (vertical 1080×1920, for example) with `--size WxH` on the render tools.
15	- Voice and subtitles in the language the user writes in. Subtitles burned in and exported as `.srt`.
16	- **The language on screen is the film's, not the demo's.** Many `STYLE.md` files set a Chinese line above an English line (subtitles, titles, labels): those are the two languages of our demos. A film in one language sets that line alone, in the upper line's place and size. A film in two keeps the stack, its main language on top. For another script, choose an openly licensed face of the same kind (weight, serif or sans, written or printed). The rest of the style's type stays: sizes, placement, how the text arrives.
17	- Loudness −14 LUFS.
18	
19	Say it in the questions when it matters: a good Chinese voice uses Microsoft's online service (edge-tts) and needs a connection; offline, Kokoro reads Chinese but sounds plain (TECHNIQUE.md §4).
20	
21	Requests that only change the plan:
22	
23	- **No voice, or no subtitles.** Drop those steps and say so in the treatment.
24	- **Their own voice recording.** Use it as it is; transcribe it with faster-whisper for word timings.
25	- **Their own material**: logos, photos, footage, and for a style built from real data or scans (its `STYLE.md` says so) their own data, scans, imagery or CAD. Ask whether they have any; what they give comes first, and the sources in the `STYLE.md` are the fallback. Before you download from those sources, tell the user what you will fetch, from where and under which licence. Rights: section 12.
26	
27	## 2. Find a benchmark first
28	
29	Before writing anything, pick one or two reference works (films, title sequences, games, ads) that set the bar for this style **and this topic**. They are your choice, made for the user's film; don't borrow the demo's. Write down:
30	
31	- **What to learn**: composition, pacing, camera grammar, colour logic, score structure.
32	- **What not to take**: characters, designs, melodies, specific shots, logos, fonts.
33	
34	The benchmark lifts quality more than any rule below.
35	
36	## 3. Shape the story
37	
38	- **One subject, one goal, one turn.** A character (or a single object, product or idea) wants something, something changes, it ends differently from how it began.
39	- **Hook in the first 3 seconds.** No slow logo reveal before anything happens.
40	- **An ending that echoes.** Bookend the opening, reveal the scale, or let the character do the thing right the second time.
41	- **One native move**: a moment only this medium can do (a fold that becomes a transition, ink that blooms into the next scene, a type grid that snaps into the logo). Put it at the emotional peak. `STYLE.md` lists the medium's native moves; pick or invent the one your story needs.
42	- **Cut the extras.** One gag the audience reads at thumbnail size beats three they can't. If a beat needs explaining, remove it.
43	
44	## 4. Write the treatment
45	
46	Write `TREATMENT.md` before drawing anything, and before you open the style's `DEMO.md` or demo code (an Edit & Documentary style gathers its material first: AGENTS.md, "Treatment first"):
47	
48	1. **Three candidate structures**, a few lines each (for example: a single journey, a before/after, a countdown, a list that turns), then the one you chose and why. Choose the opening image, the ending and the shape of the score from the topic too; the first idea that comes to mind for a style is usually its cliché.
49	2. **Logline and arc**: one sentence, then setup → turn → ending.
50	3. **Benchmark**: learn / don't learn (section 2).
51	4. **Shot list**: for every shot, the framing (wide / full / medium / close / insert), angle, camera move (push, pull, pan, track, crane, zoom), duration, and **why** it is shot that way.
52	5. **Beat sheet**, second by second.
53	6. **Cue map**: tempo, bar grid, instrumentation per section, and on which beat every cut, key action and subtitle lands.
54	7. **Sound design table**: for each section, the ambience bed, the main foley and the music state.
55	8. **Subtitle and title design**: the type is part of the style.
56	
57	## 5. Prove the look
58	
59	- **With characters**: draw a model sheet (turnaround, 3–4 expressions, 2–3 key poses, palette) plus two style frames.
60	- **Without characters**: three style frames from the film, one of them the signature shot.
61	
62	Render them with the real drawing code, not a mock-up, and check them yourself against the `STYLE.md` before going on.
63	
64	### The storyboard (only if the user asked for one)
65	
66	Render 6–9 key shots with the real drawing code, tiled into one sheet (`core/render/sheet.py`) with shot number, framing, duration and line under each. Send it with the logline and what you are least sure about, and **wait for approval**. If the user didn't ask for one, don't stop.
67	
68	## 6. Sound is half the film
69	
70	- **Every visible action has a sound**: landings, page turns, cuts, drips, clicks, cloth. Match the material (paper, wood, metal, ink and glass all sound different).
71	- **Three layers**: ambience (room, wind, rain, city), foley (tied to actions) and music. Duck the music under dialogue and key foley.
72	- **At least two real silences**, or near-silences, before the turn or the emotional peak. The first sound after the silence should be one of the most important sounds in the film.
73	- **Use sound as a transition** at least twice: bring the next scene's sound in early (J-cut) or let the last scene's sound run over the cut (L-cut).
74	- **Avoid generic "piano and strings".** Score in the instruments of the style's sound palette.
75	
76	## 7. Rhythm: the music grid comes first
77	
78	- Write the cue map before animating. The picture locks to the grid, and a script checks every cue (TECHNIQUE.md §3).
79	- **Vary the pace**: alternate fast and slow, include one clear acceleration or deceleration, and give the audience one breath (a long take or a held pause). A film at one even speed has failed.
80	- One action, one sound, one cut, but don't cut on every beat. Leave time to see.
81	- **Pace for the viewer, not the clock**:
82	  - Hold every subtitle at least 1.8 s, and never shorter than the spoken line + 0.6 s.
83	  - After text finishes animating in, hold it for roughly (letters ÷ 15 + 1.5) s in English, (characters ÷ 4.5 + 1.5) s in Chinese; `readcheck.mjs` checks this for you.
84	  - Hold a title card at least 4 s.
85	  - Give failures and gags enough time to be understood.
86	  - Fast is fine; make it fast with fewer words per screen, not by cutting before people finish reading.
87	
88	## 8. Camera: every shot needs a reason
89	
90	- Use at least **four different camera moves** and real changes of framing. 2D has a camera too: push, pull, parallax, focus pulls, frames within frames.
91	- **One signature shot** people remember: a oner, a scale reveal, a transition made from the medium itself.
92	- **Design transitions inside the medium** (a page turn, a carved line growing, ink spreading), as one consistent grammar. Avoid default fades and hard cuts.
93	- At key moments the subject fills at least a third of the frame height, with clear staging and a readable silhouette.
94	
95	## 9. Performance
96	
97	- **Anticipation, action, follow-through** on every meaningful move. Characters change emotion. They do not just slide across the screen.
98	- **Motion continuity**, especially for characters built from code rigs:
99	  - Blend every pose with keyframes and easing; never switch poses inside an `if`. The only exception is a deliberate one-frame comic pop.
100	  - Check shoulders and arms on a large action test sheet (reach, raise, run, kneel) before shooting (TECHNIQUE.md §10).
101	  - Held props sit **between the palms**, at a depth between the two arms. A hand-over interpolates from one palm to the other. A rolling object turns by distance ÷ radius.
102	  - Step through key actions at 0.2 s intervals, enlarged.
103	- Check every expression at final size, especially eyebrow direction: "worried" and "angry" are one flip apart.
104	
105	## 10. The failures we saw most
106	
107	- Subject too small, too far away, or pushed against the frame edge.
108	- Too dark to read, or a colour laid on the same colour (red on red).
109	- Subtitles covering the subject.
110	- A gag or failure too fast to understand.
111	- Blank frames in transitions.
112	- A timed effect (iris, zoom, follow cam) that doesn't track the subject after the camera moves (one world → screen function, TECHNIQUE.md §2).
113	
114	## 11. Before you deliver
115	
116	- Run the review loop (TECHNIQUE.md §8): contact sheets, 0.2 s strips of key actions, one full-speed viewing with sound.
117	- **One fix round.** Fix everything the review and the checks below find in one round, then check once more. Small fixes that second check turns up (a level, a frame) belong to the same round; anything bigger, tell the user in one line when you deliver. The user's notes after delivery are new rounds: change only what they ask.
118	- **Not the demo again.** After the treatment, read `DEMO.md` and compare: structure, opening, signature shot, camera path, score shape, ending. At least four of the six must differ; rethink the ones that match. Before delivery, put your contact sheet next to the demo poster (`styles/<slug>/poster.jpg`) as a last check.
119	- Voice: every line transcribes back correctly (speech-to-text check). For Chinese, one misheard character in a short line is normal: listen, and if it is right, let the check expect what the model heard (TECHNIQUE.md §4).
120	- Loudness about −14 LUFS; no black frames, no NaN frames; subtitles in sync and not covering key action.
121	- Every row of the sound design table is actually in the mix.
122	- Every map, globe or satellite view passes section 13, checked enlarged.
123	- No LemoLab sign-off: `grep -rniE "lemo ?lab|opus 5\.5" <project folder>` finds nothing outside `LICENSE`, `CREDITS` and the library's path in `LIB=` lines, and you have watched the last seconds of the film (text drawn into an image can't be grepped).
124	
125	**Deliver**, in the project folder (the complete list):
126	
127	- `<name>.mp4` (24 fps unless `STYLE.md` sets another rate, about −14 LUFS) and `poster.jpg`;
128	- `<name>.srt`, when the film has narration, dialogue or subtitles; when the subtitles are burned into the picture, `subtitles_<lang>.srt` instead (desktop players load a `.srt` named like the video on top of the picture, so every line would show twice);
129	- `TREATMENT.md`;
130	- `CREDITS`: every third-party asset in the film (sample libraries, music, fonts, images, the voice engine) with its source and licence (TECHNIQUE.md §11);
131	- the source, with a one-command `build.sh` (TECHNIQUE.md §2).
132	
133	**Tell the user**, in their language: where the project folder and the film are; that `CREDITS` lists the third-party assets in the film and their licences; and that they are responsible for the materials they use in it.
134	
135	## 12. Copyright red lines
136	
137	- References teach grammar only. Don't copy characters, designs, melodies, shots, logos or type designs.
138	- No existing works, games, brands or events appear in the film unless the user owns them or has the right to use them. That includes the logos, photos and footage the user hands you: use them when they say they have the right, otherwise draw fictional stand-ins.
139	- Some of our demos are unofficial fan films of real events or characters. Keep the style, and never carry those names, marks or characters into a user's film.
140	
141	## 13. Maps
142	
143	These apply to every frame that shows a map, a globe or satellite imagery, in every style.
144	
145	- **No borders unless the film is about them.** Draw coastlines, terrain, imagery or streets, without national or provincial borders. Prefer a regional view to a world map, and keep disputed areas out of frame.
146	- **When China is in frame, draw all of it.** Taiwan, Hainan, the South China Sea islands with the dashed line (in frame, or in an inset), and the Diaoyu Islands with Chiwei Yu. Taiwan and the mainland are one country, in the same colour and the same treatment. Zangnan and Aksai Chin are drawn as on China's standard map.
147	- **Default border data doesn't meet this.** The default boundaries of Natural Earth, world-atlas and OpenStreetMap can't be used to draw China. When the film needs borders, use China-view data (such as Natural Earth's `admin_0_countries_chn` layers, checked against the standard map) or China's standard map service (bzdt.ch.mnr.gov.cn).
148	- **Words follow the same map.** Taiwan, Hong Kong and Macao are never listed as countries: not in labels, legends, subtitles, the voice-over or data tables. A list that includes them is "countries and regions". Clean a dataset's country field before you chart it.
149	- **Other disputed areas**: the same; frame them out, or leave their borders undrawn.
150	- **Check and credit.** Before delivery, enlarge every map shot and check it against these rules. `CREDITS` names the map data, its source and its view (for example "Natural Earth 1:50m, China view").
151

35	## 2. The picture is a function of time
36	
37	Each film is a folder with an `index.html` (`<demo>` in the commands) that exposes:
38	
39	```js
40	window.DUR = 54.2;                 // seconds
41	window.render = (t) => { ... };    // draw the frame at time t, deterministic
42	window.READY = true;               // set once fonts and images are loaded
43	window.EV = [{t, type, ...}];      // optional: sound / cue events for the mixer
44	window.TEXTS = (t) => [{id, text, x0, y0, x1, y1}];   // optional: every text visible at t, for readcheck (pass: true = not meant to be read in full: a sign passed by, fine-print credits)
45	```
46	
47	**Paths:** pages reach library files with absolute URLs (`/core/lib.js`, `/node_modules/three/build/three.module.js`); scripts and `build.sh` use `$LIB`. Never `../..`.
48	
49	A `build.sh` that works in both modes (in skill mode, put `LIB=<path setup.sh printed>` at the top):
50	
51	```sh
52	#!/bin/sh
53	set -e
54	HERE=$(cd "$(dirname "$0")" && pwd)
55	LIB=${LIB:-$(cd "$HERE/../.." && pwd)}          # clone mode: <repo>/films/<name>/
56	export LIB
57	[ -f "$LIB/core/render/video.mjs" ] || { echo "set LIB to the library folder"; exit 1; }
58	cd "$LIB"
59	node core/render/events.mjs "$HERE"
60	node core/render/video.mjs "$HERE" --fps 24 --out "$HERE/out/video.mp4"
61	"$LIB/.venv/bin/python" "$HERE/mix.py"                               # score, foley, voice → out/mix.wav
62	sh core/render/mux.sh "$HERE/out/video.mp4" "$HERE/out/mix.wav" "$HERE/<name>.mp4" 24
63	```
64	
65	Rules that keep it reliable:
66	
67	- **Deterministic.** No `Date.now()`, no `Math.random()` without a seed (`core/lib.js` has `mulberry` and `hash`), no state carried from the previous frame. Any frame can be rendered alone, in any order, by any worker.
68	- **Canvas 2D** for most 2D styles; **three.js** for 3D (§9); **WebGL2** shaders for post passes (film damage, CRT, ink redraw).
69	- **Animate on twos where the style wants it** (12 fps stepping for stop-motion, pixel or cel looks), but keep the camera and light smooth every frame. A stepped camera reads as lag.
70	- **One world → screen function.** Any effect that follows a subject (iris, zoom, spotlight) goes through it. Never hand-type screen coordinates.
71	- **Draw for the frame you render.** The default is 1920×1080; for another size pass `--size WxH` (e.g. `1080x1920`) to every render tool and lay the page out from `innerWidth` × `innerHeight`.
72	
73	Capture (`core/render/`):
74	
75	```sh
76	node core/render/still.mjs <demo> 1.5 12 --range 0:50:2   # review stills; exits on page errors
77	node core/render/video.mjs <demo> --fps 24 --workers 3     # all frames → <demo>/out/video.mp4
78	node core/render/events.mjs <demo>                         # export DUR + EV → events.json
79	node core/render/readcheck.mjs <demo>                      # every on-screen text stays long enough to read
80	```
81	
82	To render a second version with other content, pass it to the page and give it its own output: `--q 'content=content_alt.json' --out …/alt.mp4` (the same for `events.mjs`).
83	
84	Capture is fast because of **JPEG screenshots**, **one browser per worker** and **grain added in ffmpeg**: grain drawn in the page makes every frame incompressible and slow.
85	
86	## 3. One timeline drives everything
87	
88	Keep sections, tempo, beats and hit points in one file (`timeline.js`). Export it to JSON and let the score, the mixer, the subtitles and the checks read the same numbers:
89	
90	```js
91	export const SECS = [{ id: 'chase', t: 12.0, bpm: 144, beats: 12 }, ...];
92	export const HIT  = { pratfall: ['chase', 6], ... };   // section + beat
93	```
94	
95	A small script (`cuecheck.py`, in `styles/<slug>/demo/tools/` of several demos) compares every visual hit with the music cue it should land on. Aim for 0 ms.
96	
97	## 4. Voice
98	
99	- **TTS is only the default.** If the user brings a recording or names a voice, use that. Otherwise:
100	  - **English**: [Kokoro](https://github.com/thewh1teagle/kokoro-onnx), local, many voices (an unknown `voice` name makes `tts.py` print the full list; `af_` / `am_` are American, `bf_` / `bm_` British; cast the narrator for this film, not the demo's). `core/tts/tts.py lines.json out/` writes one WAV per line and a durations file. Its Chinese voices (`"lang": "cmn"`) work offline but sound plain.
101	  - **Chinese**: `core/tts/tts_zh.py lines.json out/` uses [edge-tts](https://github.com/rany2/edge-tts) with Microsoft's neural voices (`zh-CN-XiaoxiaoNeural`, `zh-CN-YunxiNeural`…), with the same outputs as `tts.py`, a rate per line and the silence trimmed. **It needs a network connection.**
102	- Spell numbers out in the TTS text and write them as digits in the subtitles.
103	- **Check every line**: `core/tts/asr_check.py` transcribes each WAV with faster-whisper and compares it with the script (`--lang zh`: numbers by value, so 十九 matches 19, and the rest character by character); re-generate until it exits 0. A misheard character in a short Chinese line is normal: listen, and if it is right, put what the model heard in the line's `asr` field. It also writes word timestamps for placing lines and subtitles.
104	- **Before mixing**: TTS has a high peak-to-average ratio. Compress the voice first, then balance by RMS: voice about 10 dB above the music.
105	
106	## 5. Music
107	
108	Write an original score from the cue map, in the instruments of the style's sound palette; no generic piano and strings.
109	
110	- **Samples**: `core/audio/sampler.py` plays real instruments from free libraries (VSCO 2 CE, VCSL, FreePats, Karoryfer, Salamander Grand Piano; list and licences in `core/audio/INSTRUMENTS.md`). Write the score as events `(time, instrument, pitch, duration, velocity, pan)`. Long notes are extended seamlessly, and round-robins avoid the machine-gun effect.
111	- **Plucked and folk strings** (guqin, pipa, shamisen, banjo…): `core/audio/pluck.py`, physical modelling (Karplus–Strong) with bends and vibrato.
112	- **Synthesis** with numpy for chip tunes, drones and effects; no download needed.
113	- **Balance the low end.** Synthetic scores get bass-heavy quickly. Measure energy per band after mixing; keep 20–120 Hz around −3 dB relative to the rest, skip pad notes below MIDI 48, and give the bass some 2nd and 3rd harmonics so it speaks on small speakers.
114	
115	## 6. Sound effects and mix
116	
117	- `core/audio/sfx.py` synthesises foley procedurally (click, whoosh, thump, ding, paper, noise beds…) with filters, envelopes and `add(buffer, sound, at, gain, pan)`. Drive it from `window.EV`, so every sound sits exactly on its frame.
118	- **Master**: `sh core/render/mux.sh video.mp4 mix.wav out.mp4 24 [grain]` muxes, runs a two-pass loudnorm to −14 LUFS with a true-peak limit, adds grain in ffmpeg and prints the measured loudness; it exits non-zero on any failure. On light backgrounds use less grain; for pixel and vector styles, none.
119	- Films with grain baked into the picture compress badly; re-encode with `-tune grain` and a higher CRF.
120	
121	## 7. Subtitles
122	
123	- Export `.srt` with `core/render/srt.py cues.json out.srt` (cues = `[{t0, t1, text}]`), and burn styled captions into the page itself: the caption design is part of the style.
124	- Timing rules are in DIRECTOR.md §7.
125	
126	## 8. Review loop
127	
128	1. Contact sheets: a frame every 1–2 s with `still.mjs --range`, tiled with `core/render/sheet.py`. At least two full passes.
129	2. Frame strips at 0.2 s for every key action: hand-overs, falls, hits.
130	3. On the final file: `ffmpeg -af ebur128` (loudness), `blackdetect` (blank frames), whisper again on the final mix if it has voice.
131	4. Watch it once, at full speed, with sound.
132	
133	## 9. 3D notes
134	
135	- three.js r170 rendered headless through WebGL2 on the GPU; physical depth of field and GTAO from `core/three/post.js`, rendered at 2× and downsampled.
136	- Lighting: soft area lights plus a Poly Haven HDRI at low intensity reads more "real" than bright ambient light.
137	- `core/three/post.js` is written for a perspective camera. For an orthographic camera swap `perspectiveDepthToViewZ` for `orthographicDepthToViewZ` in its depth pass, or the depth of field silently breaks.
138	
139	## 10. Characters drawn in code
140	
141	- A 2.5D rig (torso, head, limbs solved per frame) is enough for pantomime.
142	- Order the shoulder rotation as abduction, then flexion; the reverse order crosses raised arms into an X.
143	- Let the shoulder girdle rise and move forward as the arm lifts, and don't outline the part of the arm that overlaps the torso: that line is what makes a joint look like a puppet seam.
144	
145	## 11. Assets, credits and fonts
146	
147	Only CC0, CC BY or OFL material, each listed in the film's `CREDITS` with its source and licence; `core/audio/sampler.py credits(names)` writes the lines for the instruments you used. Public-domain works count as CC0; "no known restrictions" does not. Data or images under other open licences (ODbL, CC BY-SA, open-hardware licences) only after you have named the licence and its terms (attribution, share-alike) to the user and they agree. The user's own material is fine as it is. Images from an image generator (the ✦ styles) are listed too: which tool and model made them, that they are generated, and where the prompts are kept; drawings the user made are credited to them.
148	
149	A film that states facts (a style built from real data or scans: its `STYLE.md` says so) keeps a `FACTS.md` in the project folder: each claim with its source URL and the quoted wording, or the measurement that produced it.
150	
151	Fonts: Google Fonts (OFL), self-hosted in the project. The typefaces a `STYLE.md` names are not in the library; download them (`https://github.com/google/fonts/tree/main/ofl/<family>`) into the project's `fonts/`. `core/fonts/` holds a few Latin display fonts and a Chinese display font with only about 200 glyphs, not enough for running Chinese text. For Chinese, subset a CJK font to the characters you use: the Google Fonts CSS API with `&text=` returns just those glyphs (`https://fonts.googleapis.com/css2?family=Noto+Sans+SC:wght@700&text=<URL-encoded characters>`). Download the font file it points to into the project's `fonts/` and load it with `@font-face`; don't link Google Fonts at render time.
152	
153	## 12. Where to look in our demos
154	
155	| If you need… | Look at |
156	|---|---|
157	| 2D character animation and lip sync | `styles/scifi-toon/`, `styles/cel-anime-80s/` |
158	| a timeline-driven score with cue checking | `styles/microgame/`, `styles/silent-film/` |
159	| an image-to-ink redraw and film-damage post pass | `styles/silent-film/demo/engine/` |
160	| a brush or stroke engine | `styles/watercolor/`, `styles/ink-wash/`, `styles/impasto/` |
161	| 3D with depth of field and real materials | `styles/brick-toy/`, `styles/paper-popup/` |
162	| a CRT or VHS look | `core/post/crt.js`, `styles/ascii-crt/`, `styles/backrooms/` |
163	
164	Each style's `DEMO.md` says how its demo was built. Open it and the code only after your treatment exists, to learn a technique, never to rebuild our film (an Edit & Documentary style's material tools in `demo/tools/` come first: AGENTS.md, "Treatment first"). In skill mode, get the source with `sh <skill folder>/scripts/setup.sh demo <slug>`. Copied demo code often reaches the library with `../..`: replace that with `$LIB` or absolute URLs.
165

8:A miniature world built from **flat-shaded low-poly geometry** (hexagonal tile columns, box buildings with prism roofs, cone and icosahedron trees) floating in a faceted sea or void, watched by an **orthographic camera** at an isometric angle. No perspective and no horizon: distance dissolves into a **screen-space sky gradient**, so the world looks like a model suspended in colour. **Light, not texture, tells time**: every facet changes colour as the sun moves; in the dark only emissive blocks keep their colour.
20:- **Light beams** (searchlight, projector, torch): a camera-facing ribbon with a Gaussian profile, bright at the root and fading with distance, plus a wider faint halo copy; light the surface under it in its own shader.
26:- **At night, warm emissives are the only bright things** (windows, lamps, a beam). Keep the sun sideways to the camera in key shots (low sun behind the target turns faceted water into glare); water receives no shadows.
34:- **Subtitles**: no box; warm white with a soft dark-blue drop shadow, centred low; a small flat-shaded tile icon beside them whose top colour follows the time of day. Hold ≥ max(1.8 s, speech + 0.6 s), never overlapping the next line or a title.
48:## 6. Camera grammar
50:`THREE.OrthographicCamera`. **Frustum height is the zoom** (a few units for a close-up, the whole world at a dozen or more, hundreds for a scale reveal); place the camera ≥ 3 × frustum height away or the bottom of the frame looks under the sea. A vocabulary, not a route. Opening and ending come from the topic.
61:| Time-lapse sun sweep, camera still | light is the time machine | a day; a season; history |
63:Intercut wide and close on beats: wide shows the shape growing, close sells the bounce. Transitions: hard cuts on the beat, a time-of-day change, a zoom through the sky; no dissolves, no perspective whip-pans.
72:- **Voice**: clear and gentle, few short lines; avoid words that collide with the film's subject (a film about baking: "flour" heard as "flower").
88:- `perspectiveDepthToViewZ` in shared post code is wrong for an orthographic camera → `orthographicDepthToViewZ`.
91:- A double-sided additive cone reads as two white lines → a camera-facing Gaussian ribbon + halo.
92:- Camera too close for its frustum → the frame bottom shows below the sea → distance ≥ 3 × frustum height.
98:In `demo/` (three.js): `world.js` (hex layout, primitive props, growth schedule → events with notes, arrival curves), `sea.js` (faceted wave shader, shallow map, beam-lit water), `post.js` (ortho post: GTAO → sky/haze + stars → tilt-shift → bloom → grade), `story.js` (beat grid, time-of-day keyframes, shots), `main.js` (renderer, lights, per-shot cameras, HUD, event export), `music/score.py` (event-driven score; `music/check.py` compares audio onsets and pitches with the events), `mix.py` (foley, beds, ducking). File map and build steps: DEMO.md.
102:You decide the world (island, town, orchard, factory floor, planet), what grows or changes, the palette within the colour logic, the opening, the ending, the camera path and the pacing. All far from our demo:
110:How our demo was made (story, shots, score, end card, build): [DEMO.md](DEMO.md). Read it after your treatment exists.

// take the k-th note of the chord at time t that falls within [lo,hi] (k is a contour value in 0..1)
